intro: A long violin melody grows into Wagner’s birthday greeting for Cosima: a lullaby, a horn call and a bird in the branches. Stanley Chapple conducts the Modern Chamber Orchestra in this 1925 recording.

sections.label: A · A violin begins the greeting
sections.mNote: The violin’s long E-major phrase gathers other strings around it

sections.label: A′ · The opening tune grows
sections.mNote: Strings and wind share the long melody

sections.label: B · An oboe lullaby
sections.mNote: The oboe sings above little detached string figures

sections.label: Dev · Horn and clarinet entwine
sections.mNote: Wind melodies cross the strings’ flowing lines

sections.label: C · Siegfried and the Woodbird
sections.mNote: A horn song meets quick clarinet and flute calls

sections.label: A″ · The long melody returns
sections.mNote: The opening string tune returns among the other melodies

sections.label: Coda · The house grows quiet
sections.mNote: Strings and a low horn linger over E

cues.title: One violin line unfolds
cues.text: The first violins begin alone, softly. Violas and cellos enter beneath the held note, then the second violins add their own moving line. The double bass waits. Wagner lets the E-major melody find its feet without a heavy step underneath it.
cues.evidence: Wagner, Siegfried-Idyll, Schott full score, 1878, plate 22430, p. 1: Ruhig bewegt, successive string entries, double bass silent. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/20380.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Musicians on the staircase
cues.text: On Christmas morning, 1870, thirteen musicians stand on the stairs at Tribschen while Cosima wakes upstairs. “Music was sounding, and such music,” she writes in her diary. When it ends, Wagner enters with the five children and gives her the score.
cues.evidence: Cosima Wagner’s diary, 25 December 1870, English extract in the Verdehr Trio programme note: https://verdehr.com/notes-WagnerSiegfriedIdyll.pdf. Gerald Larner identifies the thirteen players and staircase: https://geraldlarner.com/work/wagner-siegfried-idyll.

cues.title: A quartet never finished
cues.text: The opening melody has a private history. Wagner first imagines it for a string quartet for Cosima in 1864. The quartet remains unfinished; the tune finds another home in Brünnhilde’s music in Siegfried, and then in this family greeting.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, Siegfried Idyll programme note: the projected 1864 quartet, its dedication to Cosima, and the theme’s later use in Siegfried, Act III. https://geraldlarner.com/work/wagner-siegfried-idyll.

cues.title: The oboe sings simply
cues.text: Wagner marks the oboe’s lullaby Sehr einfach — very simply. Its short phrases sit above little detached notes in the violins, then the lower strings. The oboe sounds as though it could carry on singing with no orchestra at all.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, p. 12, oboe entry marked Sehr einfach and detached string accompaniment. Gerald Larner identifies the traditional German lullaby and its association with Wagner’s daughter Eva.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melodies share the room
cues.text: The tunes begin to overlap. A wind instrument can hold a phrase while a string line turns beneath it; fragments of the opening melody fit around the lullaby. Wagner makes the small orchestra busy without filling every space.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, middle span, including p. 24: horn, clarinet and independent string lines. Gerald Larner describes the combination and inversion of the opening theme and lullaby. This note concerns the recurring counterpoint, not a single entrance.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Fidi’s birdsong and a sunrise
cues.text: The original title is Tribschener Idyll mit Fidi-Vogelgesang und Orange-Sonnenaufgang: Tribschen Idyll with Fidi’s Birdsong and Orange Sunrise. Fidi is the family’s nickname for their son Siegfried, born in June 1869. The name Siegfried Idyll points at once to the son and to the opera.
cues.evidence: Rainer Fineske, for the International Association of Wagner Societies, on the work’s 150th anniversary: the original title, Fidi as Siegfried, and the link with the opera; Siegfried’s birth on 6 June 1869 in the Richard Wagner Museum’s account of the Tribschen years. https://www.richard-wagner.org/rwvi/en/news/news-committee/?collection_id=3075 https://www.richard-wagner-museum.ch/en/museum/years-in-lucerne/

cues.title: A horn and a bird
cues.text: A horn sings Siegfried’s tune in C major. The clarinet and flute answer with quick Woodbird figures, marked lustig — merrily. For a moment, the family room opens onto the forest of Siegfried.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, pp. 28–29: Lebhaft in C major, horn melody followed by clarinet and flute figures marked lustig. The operatic themes are identified in Gerald Larner’s programme note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The birthday gift goes public
cues.text: Financial pressure brings the family’s music to the publisher. Wagner sells the Idyll to Schott; the score appears in 1878. A piece first played on a staircase can now travel to concert halls, carrying its lullaby with it.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner on the sale under financial pressure: https://geraldlarner.com/work/wagner-siegfried-idyll. Schott’s first full-score edition is dated 1878 in the Sibley catalogue: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/20380.

cues.title: Witness, then trumpeter
cues.text: On 25 August 1870, four months before the staircase, Wagner and Cosima marry; Hans Richter is one of the two witnesses. Richter, who copies Wagner’s scores, learns the trumpet specially for the birthday performance. Its part lasts thirteen bars.
cues.evidence: Richard Wagner Museum, Lucerne: the wedding of 25 August 1870 and its witnesses, Malwida von Meysenbug and Hans Richter. Richter as Wagner’s copyist and the trumpeter of the first performance: Mahler Foundation biography. He learned the trumpet for the occasion: Concise Oxford Dictionary of Music. A trumpet part of only 13 bars: Rainer Fineske, International Association of Wagner Societies. https://www.richard-wagner-museum.ch/en/museum/years-in-lucerne/ https://www.mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/contemporaries/hans-richter https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/siegfried-idyll https://www.richard-wagner.org/rwvi/en/news/news-committee/?collection_id=3075

cues.title: A low E remains
cues.text: The double bass holds E. A low horn note stays with it while the strings make their last small turns. At the end, the resting wind players join the E-major chord, pianissimo. The greeting closes as gently as it began.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, p. 46: sustained E in double bass and second horn, moving string fragments, final pp wind entry and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The oboe takes up a lullaby
transitions.how: The horns finish their phrase and fall silent. A few plucked bass notes accompany the strings’ quiet link towards the B-major lullaby. The oboe begins Sehr einfach, with detached violin figures underneath. Soon the bass rests altogether: the tune has room to breathe.
transitions.evidence: Schott full score, p. 12: diminuendo, pizzicato bass, oboe Sehr einfach and detached violin accompaniment. The recording’s section boundary locates the approach to this passage.

transitions.title: The horn opens a forest scene
transitions.how: The flute and violins finish their quick descending figures. Wagner clears away the strings and writes Lebhaft in C major. One horn holds the bass beneath the other’s song; clarinet and flute then answer with the Woodbird’s quick triplets.
transitions.evidence: Schott full score, pp. 28–29, change to Lebhaft, horn duet and subsequent clarinet and flute entries.

transitions.title: The bass settles on E
transitions.how: Wagner gradually slows the last string phrases, first Rallentando, then Bedeutend langsamer — considerably slower. A low horn sustains E as the double bass takes up the same pedal. Little pieces of the melody continue above it, with the strings marked immer pp.
transitions.evidence: Schott full score, pp. 45–46. The named markings and E pedal belong to the closing section; the section boundary marks its approach.

source.title: Siegfried-Idyll — Schott full score, 1878, plate 22430
source.locator: Printed pp. 1, 4, 8, 12, 24, 28, 31–32, 36, 45–46. Approximate score regions; the 1925 session’s exact staffing is not documented.

timeline.note: Opening string span, p. 1; basses and winds are initially silent in the published score.
Approximate opening expansion, pp. 4–8: woodwinds, horns and basses progressively join the string texture. The 1:06 audio boundary marks the broad region, not simultaneous or bar-aligned entrances.
Approximate contrasting-song region, p. 12: the oboe’s simply marked lullaby emerges from a reduced texture.
Approximate combination region, p. 24: horn line, clarinet support and mobile strings.
Approximate animated region, p. 28: horn call and flute forest-bird figure; these are not simultaneous throughout the span.
Central stronger region, pp. 31–32. Trumpet reinforcement is brief, not continuous for the entire span.
Approximate later recollection, p. 36: light wind exchanges above returning string movement.
Closing region, pp. 45–46: horn and bassoon support around sustained strings. Flute, oboe and clarinets join only the final chord, not the whole preceding conclusion; trumpet remains silent.

composer.epithet: He hid the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth and taught it to remember everything his characters wanted to forget.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no success worth mentioning. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons calling across the strings’ storm. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to persuade somebody to stage his music.

He had grown up inside the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies supplied the sounds; Theodor Weinlig supplied counterpoint lessons in 1831. Jobs followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen remained unperformed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, collapsed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
